The presence of dense star clusters containing a high proportion of massive stars at the centers of galaxies is an enigma, and some theories attribute their existence to remnants of early star populations. One such theory posits that the initial stars may have formed binaries that, through gravitational interactions, were broken apart, leaving the more massive components in the star cluster. We investigate the validity of this theory by comparing its predictions with the gravitational wave signals detected by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA. Our simulations reveal that this scenario produces a distinctive pattern of gravitational wave events that differ from those produced by random distributions of early stars. Unfortunately, distinguishing between the two scenarios will require more precise measurements from current and future detectors.

Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is widely used in next-generation wireless networks due to its superior performance and resistance to distortions caused by multipath propagation. Despite its many benefits, the actual performance of OFDM systems falls short of the theory because real-world radio channels introduce non-linear effects. To mitigate these impacts, we investigate an advanced wireless communication system that utilizes frequency-selective analog circuitry and multiple OFDM transmit antennas to securely transmit data to multiple receivers. By drawing on both short-term and long-term characteristics of the wireless channel, we develop a method for optimizing power distribution across transmit antennas in order to maximize reception rates while adhering to constraints on circuit distortion and power consumption. This result is both efficient for real-time implementation and includes a novel way of converting reception maximization into an optimization problem with convex properties. Furthermore, we explore a strategy for allocating power across multiple OFDM subcarriers in order to find a efficient balance between performance and power consumption. Numerical tests demonstrate the significant security benefits of this multi-carrier system in real-world applications.

Text-based adventure games present a simple world structure, making them suitable for achieving high-level performance. This paper introduces an agent for text-based adventure games that achieves record-breaking results. At a comparable performance level to the current best contender, it uses one million GPU seconds with a six-layer transformer model. In contrast, it also demonstrates that it can tackle larger games effectively using only one hundred thousand GPU seconds at a six-layer transformer performance level.

Deep learning methods, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved significant success in various sequential data analysis tasks. However, their practical application is hindered by slow processing speeds and excessive power consumption. This study explores multiple strategies to accelerate and reduce power consumption of LSTM models, including an optimized hardware design specifically tailored to the structure of the LSTM architecture and its accompanying control unit, as well as a novel hardware reduction technique based on hierarchical compressed tensor factorization. When applied to video id, experiments demonstrated that this technique minimizes weight storage requirements and accelerates processing speeds of LSTM models, outperforming traditional compressed approaches. Notably, an accurate and efficient hardware system utilizing this technique was deployed on actual hardware to process real-world video sequences.

We observe that the feeble gravity conjecture, which posits an upper limit on a state's charge-to-mass ratio in relation to the lightest particle's ratio, can be subdivided into two distinct categories. The first category asserts the convexity of the set of all possible state configurations, while there is no universally accepted definition for this property's criteria and general proof. Alternatively, we interpret it as the feeble gravity conjecture's subset implying that all state configurations possess a minimum charge-to-mass ratio, which we refer to as the robust gravity conjecture. There is an established relationship demonstrating how this subset interpretation connects to its particle counterpart. However, we provide evidence suggesting that the convexity of the set of all possible state configurations constitutes a novel concept. We also explore the interplay between these two interpretations under transformations that combine states and lower the system's mass threshold. In the context of conformal field theories, we demonstrate that the robust gravity conjecture is automatically met, but we find that the convexity of the set of all possible state configurations is not inherently guaranteed. We further propose that achieving convexity of the set of all possible state configurations might constitute a new, meaningful principle that could be regarded as a more comprehensive version of the feeble gravity conjecture.

Hochster recently proved the Hilbert polynomial of the cohomology of a graded piece of a graded ring is invariant under extension to a larger ring with the same field. We demonstrate that a local ring containing a field is F-pure or F-rational if and only if its Hilbert function or local cohomology's polynomial has compact support, providing a new characterization in multiple ways. Additionally, we establish conditions for the graded pieces of the associated graded ring at a maximal ideal of a two-variable power series ring to have finite dimensional local cohomology, generalizing prior work and implying that certain rings are F-rational if they are quotients of these rings with specific degree conditions.

The research community has been actively exploring various aspects of hydrogen fuel cell technology, wind turbine systems and compressed air storage in recent years. While these technologies have been compared individually, there's no available data that directly contrasts them all together in a single study. In order to address this knowledge gap, we used proton exchange membrane fuel cell, permanent magnet generator and adiabatic compressed air as standalone systems to create a direct comparison between the three technologies. In order to assess the market engagement influence on policy formulation, a Markov decision process was utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of policy options that reflect real-world market involvement. The research reveals that although hydrogen fuel cell technology is better suited for applications with high energy requirements, integrating real-world market engagement into policy formulation enhances the effectiveness of the resulting policies.

Let p(x) and q(x) be relatively prime polynomials over an field K. Under the condition that p(q(x)) and q(p(x)) are also relatively prime, we investigate the structure of triples (f_n(x), f_m(x), p_nq_m(x)) in the monic polynomial pair (p_n(x), q_n(x)) generated by the iterates of the Newton's method. The positions n and m that ensure common factors between q(p)^n and p(q)^m depend on a generalized remainder theorem and a unique representation of the polynomial ideal. For the case where p and q are quadratic, we can compute a specific ratio m/n using the Euclidean algorithm. The results for the polynomial ideal allow us to express the greatest common divisor p_n(x) and q_m(x) as a combination of p_n(x) and q_m(x).

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by exceptionally high-speed winds and temperature conditions that are nearing those of radiative-equilibrium in its northern region. A large-scale warm anomaly has been observed at high latitudes near the equator, preparing for the development of the permanent polar stratospheric vortex located in the northern pole. This development is anticipated to occur during a specific period of time, as predicted by both theoretical models and numerical simulations. Researchers have identified an unusual hexagonal shape in the northern atmosphere that is believed to be a direct precursor to the vortex's formation, encompassing the boundary between cold and warm air masses in the planet's upper atmosphere. The characteristics of this hexagonal shape are being compared to previous observations and those of the upcoming mission.

We consider a Schrödinger equation with a convex confinement outside of a convex obstacle. It is shown that a solution with an initially high energy state, exceeding a threshold related to the curvature of the convex obstacle, will inevitably explode. By modifying the equation to include a logarithmic nonlinearity withAssumption (A), the explosion of such high energy solutions is proven. The result extends previous findings, which required the confinement to be unbounded in all directions, and relies on the development of sharp a priori estimates and the establishment of an explosion criterion based on energy bounds.

We provide proof for the existence of certain efficient varieties transformations, known as local abbreviations, within positive-characteristic fields, extending previous findings that were restricted to varieties over fields of characteristic zero. These abbreviations, when applied to freely produced algebras, result in an equally produced target algebra and maintain a fundamental property, such that the target algebra can be accessed via a constrained set of rules from the source algebra. Our work builds on a generalised abbreviation concept, extending standard reformulations and condensing strategies, with relevant applications in Inference, Optimization, and summarization. Our results are grounded in automata theory, model theory, and universal algebra.

In the context of representation theory, we have established an adjustment to Serre's classic collection concept, introducing a "graded collection" definition and subsequent polarization and un-polarization processes. These procedures allow for the reversal of a graded collection's orientation. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the composition of two collections corresponds to a form of convolution, with a connection to the Hall algebra being drawn from a prior study. Notably, the degree of polarization is observable in the resulting convolution outcome.

This informal note explores the standardization of measures in the context of orbital integrals. We begin by examining measures from steinberg's work and then move on to the more recent and more flexible framework established by Langlands and Takeda. We highlight the key distinctions and relationships between these two frameworks. Specifically, we investigate how the measures defined by Langlands and Takeda relate to those of steinberg through local factors that can be interpreted as elements of the Grothendieck group of a group.

Research on scattering has been enhanced by introducing a novel concept involving the phase information of a specific Bessel function in a toroidal geometry. Utilizing near-edge x-ray absorption spectroscopy, we targeted a Carbon K-edge absorption feature within a graphene sample and identified the phase information of a particular signal corresponding to a Bessel function, $J_0$, within the experiment's coordinate system. Our findings confirmed that this phase information accurately matches that of $J_0$ and was made possible by focusing on the phase characteristics of x-ray reflection. By gathering multiple datasets at varying incidence angles, we were able to extract this information, which is typically lost during standard experiments, providing valuable insights into the behavior of matter.

A new and efficient approach is proposed to model single-phase Darcy flow in fractured and homogeneous media. This method combines two existing approach, specifically the finite element method for the TD1 problem and a hybrid complementary finite element technique for a local problem around fracture interfaces. By leveraging the high permeability in the matrix, interface conditions are approximated using an asymptotic problem, which allows us to discard the complex fractured model and replace it with a source term in a homogeneous environment. This technique eliminates the need to employ small finite elements around the interface, rather an integral term is computed numerically and added to the form bilinear form. This technique is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the interface interface is more complex and extends further than the current technique's application. Furthermore, we obtain a quantitative estimate of the error and establish the technique's convergence properties. This method is also easy to implement as it leverages the existing finite element code for resolution.

The Bayes factor stands out as a prominent alternative to p-values in the current statistical debate, offering an unbiased method for hypothesis testing that incorporates the results of repeated experiments efficiently. However, the Bayes factor's performance lags behind traditional methods like t-tests in certain scenarios, specifically when multiple studies are conducted and prior information needs to be updated accordingly. This paper aims to provide a practical guide for implementing the Bayes factor in large-scale experimental workflows by utilizing the R programming language and the Casper framework. It involves writing Bayesian models with the Stan compiler and running a series of examples to unlock the full potential of the Bayes factor in workflow-based research.

Research on functional indicators has explored how certain words, such as conjunctions and prepositions, can assist in machine learning tasks by providing additional information beyond their grammatical function. This paper introduces a comprehensive English dictionary containing 2,000 words classified according to their associated discourse information, enabling the visualization and manipulation of discourse spaces. It also presents Discourse Sense Verification, an application that leverages this discourse information to automatically derive word senses using a pre-trained word vector model and topic modeling techniques. Experimental results show that nine out of all evaluated indicators outperform baseline methods in identifying word senses accurately, with an F-score of 0.78. The discourse indicator framework and DiscSense application provide a foundation for more sophisticated models of human language meaning that incorporate information exchange aspects.

From the simplest convex optimization, where a function is directly minimized on a Euclidean space, to the most common nonconvex case, where a function maintains a "convex-like" property known as geodesic convexity across its entire solution landscape on a manifold, functions can be categorized by their difficult levels. Now, a novel difficulty has been discovered for a wide range of problems when a function's global landscape is analyzed: global convexity is shown for nonconvex low-rank matrix decomposition, but for some problems, their landscapes are shown to be even more challenging due to their "worldwide convex" property. A groundbreaking research reveals that for a broad class of matrix factorization problems, the nonconvex nature of trying to recover a target matrix from its given entries by parameterizing the target matrix through the product of two matrices can, in many instances, be shown to be "geodesically convex" across its nonconvex landscape, after establishing its equivalence to a previously unstated problem. A simple proof technique is used to establish global convexity of these landscapes for a wide array of problems, including matrix completion, robust PCA, and other related nonconvex programs, providing a more efficient global optimization technique for a wide range of factorization problems.

Tiling a graph with copies of a specific subgraph is equivalent to decomposing the graph's edges into multiple subgraph copies. While this problem can be tackled by first coloring the graph's edges and then analyzing its colorings, it is often the case that determining if a graph can be tiled is a less stringent condition than creating a robust solution where the graph can be easily tiled. In 1981, Aldred et al. established a method to consistently 3-edge-color a large class of bipartite graphs without separating the graph, but in this paper, we present a counterexample that demonstrates the necessity of our edge-tinting algorithm for the presented graph. Additionally, we discuss the distinction between the problems of deciding if a graph can be tiled and doing so in a robust manner.

Various evolutionary optimization methods have been independently utilized to attain a Nash Equilibrium in non-stationary, multi-agent decision-making environments. This study examines the capability of evolutionary algorithms to facilitate a self-teaching agent in establishing a Nash Equilibrium within a repeated, symmetrical Cournot game. Initially, it determines if a MPE-based self-learning strategy can result in a stable performance and production levels around the Nash Equilibrium. Moreover, it investigates the feasibility of developing a competitive self-learning agent capable of adhering to the Nash Equilibrium principles. Our analysis reveals that a stable environment allows a self-teaching agent to produce satisfactory outcomes aligned with the Nash Equilibrium. In contrast, in competitive settings, maintaining performance and production levels around the Nash Equilibrium proves unattainable for the same self-learning approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate the necessity of incorporating more complex self-learning agents that can produce outcomes near the Nash Equilibrium in competitive scenarios.

For any directed graph with associated weights on its edges, both the fundamental properties and the symbolic power characteristics of the ideal generated by that graph's edges are inherently connected and stable under changes in those weights. Additionally, these properties remain unaltered for the generic ideal of that graph when it is considered as being defined by indeterminates associated with its vertices, and both can be effectively determined using the properties of the underlying (undirected) graph, irrespective of the weights. This allows for the resolution of questions regarding the symbolic behavior of edge ideals in weighted directed graphs and the generic ideal of a graph in determinates, extending previous results from ideals formed by undirected graphs. Notably, a new criterion is established for the equality of the square of the ideal and its first symbolic power for these weights, and both properties are characterized for the generic ideal of a directed path.

The successful application of machine learning systems depends on their ability to maintain security and reliability. A critical aspect of this is ensuring that these systems can withstand various types of attacks and failures. A key area of research is verifying the safety and dependability of artificial intelligence. In the context of deep learning, it has been established that certain adversarial inputs, even those caused by hardware malfunctions, do not cause harmful effects if the activated values stay within acceptable limits. A control mechanism is proposed to detect and prevent issues when the activated values exceed these limits. This mechanism is carefully designed to minimize any negative impact on the speed and accuracy of these systems, including those run on imperfect hardware. A case ccausating floating point errors and an example causing execution faults are caused by hardware issues. The control mechanism is compared to other methods and found to be more effective at correcting errors and preventing faulty decisions. This control mechanism is found to be successful at preventing incorrect outcomes and system crashes caused by hardware issues.

A family of Jordanian twists is constructed and analyzed, extending the original Jordanian twist implementation by Jordan and Masuoka. This family is characterized by exploring its connection to the Kirillov Reshuffle. Additionally, the family is shown to correspond to the deformation operators introduced by Kassel and Smirnov, which preserve the bialgebra structure.

Clustering words that share similar meanings can be accomplished without relying on labeled data, but most approaches either produce results specific to a particular language or require significant computational resources. In this work, we investigate a method to generate a unified semantic cluster structure across multiple languages, employing a two-stage process. Initially, we establish a conceptual framework that preserves the characteristic self-organsing property found in unsupervised learning, and then adapt it to a specific language while keeping the framework's structure intact. To implement this, we propose a novel two-stage procedure: we create a temporary intermediary language, and then directly translate the cluster structure from this language to the target language. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments in various language combinations and the results show that this method outperforms existing multi-domain clustering techniques and provides a robust, generalizable shared semantic framework.

The L3He@SPS fixed target experiment has been designed to gain knowledge in the pQCD threshold region for rare light particle production with its high sensitivity to rare light hadrons. It aims to create conditions mimicking those of small-nuclei Pb- Pb collisions at 32 A TeV, with a primary focus on pions, kaons, protons and $\phi$ mesons, by analyzing Pb- Pb collisions at 5.44 A TeV using the SPS collider.  To validate its approach, it is essential to develop an accurate prediction of the absolute cross sections for rare light hadrons produced in high-energy Pb- Pb collisions.  This paper calculates the absolute yields of pions, $\rm K^+$, $\rm K^0_S$, p and $\bar{\rm p}$ in 5.44 A TeV Xe- Xe collisions using a thermal model, a coalescence model and a RQGD model.  These results can be utilized as an initial framework for the analysis planned by the L3He- Pb experiment for low-multiplicity data, with a subsequent analysis of correlation and flow phenomena among rare light hadrons in intermediate multiplicity events.  This analysis requires a precise understanding of single-particle production in high-energy fixed target conditions.

In 2019, Chile experienced six months of intense unrest marked by daily demonstrations in Santiago and other regions, ultimately leading to the resignation of President Bachelet and significant political and economic repercussions for the country's stability. This study employs an epidemiological modeling technique to analyze the spread of unrest during this period. A statistical analysis of social media data from Twitter yielded key parameters for the model, which successfully replicated the reported protest attendance figures with high precision. The model's output highlights the rapid transmission of unrest within Santiago within one to one-and-a-half days, as well as its slower propagation to other parts of the country over the following days to weeks. The comprehensive dataset generated by this model over one-year period provides a complete profile of daily protest activity across the country, revealing the primary hotspots of unrest and offering valuable insights for policymakers and researchers aiming to prevent future occurrences.

This research develops a symbolic method for determining if inclusion relationships hold between two complex expressions, which depend on strings of finite alphabets. These expressions, known as inclusion problems, can be simplified to whether one automaton is contained within another. To achieve this, we propose the use of closure operations and intersection findings on expressions to narrow the inclusion problem to finite automaton containment, which can then be resolved using existing techniques. To do this, we first translate the expressions into a specific type of vector based automaton, which helps in applying existing methods to find the closure of expressions and their intersection. Once the closure and intersection operations have been applied, the inclusion problem is equivalent to checking if a certain type of vector based automaton is contained within a universal automaton, which can be decided using existing algorithms. Ultimately, this method provides a comprehensive solution for determining if two complex expressions are equivalent or if one is contained within the other, which has applications in various fields, including compiler optimization and access control policy analysis.

Given the demand for capability in autonomous systems to operate in diverse and ever-changing environments, our study presents the EMA-VIO model, which presents significant progress in the field of navigation by fusing deep visual understanding with inertial data. Our approach integrates an external memory module based on attention mechanisms with a micro inertial data processor. The model's capabilities are assessed through a comprehensive set of navigation tasks, demonstrating accurate visual inertia fusion, trajectory prediction, and the successful completion of novel scenarios. The EMA-VIO model's performance is superior to that of existing visual-inertial and learning-based navigation baselines, as evidenced by the results of our comprehensive ablation study.

Quantum acceleration and Berry phase effects share intriguing connections but develop independently. In this research, we introduce a new type of quantum acceleration that arises from a 3D Weyl seimimetal with a monopole-like elevated Berry curvature. This novel elevated Berry curvature monopole leads to an anomalous Hall effect, characterized by a temperature-dependent, non-Ohmic transverse voltage in flat bands. Subsequent investigations into spatial variations of this effect reveal its dependence on the Fermi level. Furthermore, we identify two distinct types of elevated-Weyl arcs on the surface, which exhibit independent 半球 monopole-like distributions and induce local variations of the anomalous Hall effect. To achieve this theoretical prediction, we propose a Hamiltonian model and perform first-principles simulations, which demonstrate the realization of this phenomenon in a new material class through an interface between a conventional Weyl semimetal and a dielectric with an artificial magnetic field.

This study investigates the resolution of a ill-posed problem involving the
completion of incomplete data for the Maxwell equations. 
A numerical approach utilizing a quasi-reversibility method is utilized to
obtain a stable and negative source term, which helps to explain the
underlying problem. 
In the absence of a mathematical proof, experimental results are presented
to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method when implemented
numerically.

When models created by various experts are combined to form a unified model, knowing significantly more and having substantially greater storage capacity, there's a current limitation when it comes to models that have been independently trained on different devices. Specifically, if a model is being trained in an environment where it can observe other models' outputs, most aggregation methods are unsuitable due to their reliance on prior information about the datasets these models have been trained on. In this study, we develop a federated knowledge integration method, FDIA, which utilizes a fedavg-style approach to combine the models and creates a new aggregation method that leverages a neural knowledge fusion technique, also suitable for use in a settings with known partitions. Contrary to other methods, FDIA can utilize FDW as an alternative to integrate the knowledge represented by the models, without requiring any prior knowledge of the datasets they've been trained on. Through simulations, FDIA demonstrates superior performance to the current state-of-the-art models, showing up to an impressive 18% improvement in model accuracy. Moreover, the FDW approach delivers up to 20% performance gains compared to simple aggregation methods when deployed in settings with known partitions.

Researchers have identified and analyzed the average squared 2-ranks of small modular groups ($S_4$ and $A_4$) in the field of elliptic curves over quartic extensions of the rational numbers. For both extensions, it was found that the average squared 2-rank is 1, with a more in-depth local-global analysis revealing that theassumed 2-rank comprises contributions from 2, 3, and infinity. Specifically, theassumed 2-rank is 3 among $96$ primes for both extensions, with an image contribution of 1 from infinity, 1 from 2 (with varying local conditions), and no contribution from 3. Furthermore, the distribution of theassumed 2-rank across different local conditions at the prime 2 for both extensions is explored.

We investigate the rate of entropy generation in a quantum system as it moves from a state of entanglement to a separated state, specifically, two particles on a 2D holographic field theory. Using the tools of holography we calculate the entropy production rate and establish an upper limit, which is constrained by the quantum null energy condition and reflects the entanglement between the particles. We compare this constraint to a hypothesis previously proposed based on gravitational dualities, and observe that the holographic calculations support the entanglement reduction bound. We also explore how particles can maximize the rate of lost entanglement by adjusting their motion, and discover that the entropy generated is unlimited as the particles approach a null trajectory. A significant implication of this research is that in a world governed by quantum mechanics, the rate at which particles can increase the distance between themselves while remaining within the reach of causal laws is directly related to the density of entanglement they carry, and thus, the distance they can traverse while remaining connected is ultimately determined by the quantum null energy condition.

This research focuses on identifying the shortest possible time interval, $\Delta t$, required for a qubit to transition from one state to an orthogonal state, given that the initial states have an assessable level of distinguishability. We develop a method for measuring the information content of initial qubit states, taking into account a broad range of relevant duration limits found in literature. By utilizing an asymmetry monotone to quantify states, we examine and compare various limits set within the density matrix framework and within the visual representation known as the Bloch sphere. It becomes evident that limits set for gauge-invariant and Majorana-Braginskii initial conditions are not evenly matched, given their asymmetric nature leads to a lack of symmetry between them. We then present a general, asymptotically tight duration limit applicable to all possible qubit states, structured according to their asymmetry. This duration rule is demonstrated numerically through testing on specific systems.

For a positive integer $n$, let's consider the interpolation operator $L_n$ associated with Lagrange nodes $x_{kj}$ defined as $x_{kj} = \xi_k + j\tau$, where $\xi_1 < \xi_2 < \dots < \xi_m$ are distinct real numbers and $0 \leq j \leq n$ are non-negative integers. It has been established by various researchers that the norm of $L_n$, denoted as $\|L_n\|$, is bounded by $C \max \{m^{2s}, (n+1)^{r}\}$ under certain conditions. However, a specific case examined by Guo and Mu shows that the bound is actually proportional to $m^n$. This study aims to provide a simpler approach to both our earlier findings as well as those of Guo and Mu.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. To improve their performance, understanding material losses is crucial. In this work, terahertz spectroscopy was used to investigate the electromagnetic properties of lithographed transmission lines in the near-field. Studies on superconducting films and dielectric substrates reveal that both materials contribute significantly to overall losses. Specifically, aluminum exhibits high terahertz absorption, and silicon dioxide displays substantial electromagnetic activity. To minimize losses in future devices, it is essential to identify alternative, low-loss materials for both components of the resonators' environment.

This study focuses on the long-range evolution of the atmosphere of Venus and outlines critical feedback mechanisms that govern the changes in its atmosphere over time. An analytical framework is employed to identify and categorize key processes operating on various timescales, from a few days to millions of years. Notably, the study highlights the opacity of the lower atmosphere and the interaction between the atmosphere and surface of Venus, which operate on intermediate timescales and complicate atmospheric modeling. It is argued that an increase in opacity can trigger feedback loops leading to runaway effects. The study also explores alternative explanations for the loss of water from Venus and proposes that photo-dissociation and mass loss from its atmosphere may have contributed to the depletion of hydrogen and the accumulation of oxygen in the lower atmosphere of the planet.

Point processes are ideal for capturing the precise occurrence times of events, providing detailed data without ambiguity. To analyze linear relationships in point processes, traditional Bayesian regression models are commonly used. In contrast, event-based points can trigger new occurrences, making the data self-correlating in a self-exciting process. In most cases, external factors also influence point processes, necessitating a consideration of both endogenous and exogenous dynamics. We integrate the self-exciting nature of point processes with Bayesian regression by utilizing a non-linear Hawkes model. This approach enables the assessment of both self-excitation and external influences on point processes within a unified Bayesian framework. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by examining loan delinquencies in a loan portfolio.

Plasma-based systems capable of modifying the properties of high-intensity laser pulses are highly prized for creating sophisticated multi-petawatt laser arrangements. When a high-intensity pump laser interacts with a magnetized plasma, it can alter the polarization of a co-propagating probe laser, and this effect is controllable by adjusting the magnetic field and the intensity of the pump beam. Under certain conditions where the lasers and the magnetic field are aligned in a specific way, a unique phenomenon occurs where the modification and enhancement of the laser's oscillation in polarization are simultaneously maximized. This synergistic effect is attributed to the nonlinear magnetic coupling between the polarization modes. By simulating this process and directly observing it in a laboratory setting using a multi-petawatt laser setup, researchers have been able to demonstrate how this concurrent modification and enhancement can be exploited to create advanced multi-petawatt laser arrangements with multiple components interacting on the same optical path.

We analyzed the electric dipole moment of the tau lepton using 117 bn of rooted gluons and electrons at ATLAS, achieving a constraint on the tau lepton's electric dipole strength, $d_{\tau}$, at less than $8.3 \times 10^{-17}~{\rm e~cm}$, refined from the previous measurement.

For over two decades, control systems have used rank measurements to identify faults, but their performance is limited by slow decoding methods for the $l_1$ norm, resulting in conservative estimates and reduced performance. This study presents a faster decoding approach for rank errors in the $l_1$ norm by leveraging an efficient exhaustive search technique and a refined greedy method, reducing the computational load and allowing rank error decoders to be applied in real-time control system control. Furthermore, it explores the use of parallel and GPU-based implementations to further improve decoding speed. Experimentation with a testbed system demonstrates the gain in performance when using parallel and GPU-based decodings.

In the context of a unit two-dimensional conformal field theory with no global symmetries, four-point correlation functions determine rotating operator product expansion (OPE) segments, which, after averaging over all permutations of external fields, yield conformal blocks. These blocks can be mapped to the dynamics of four semi-infinite strings interacting in anti-de Sitter space through the AdS/CFT correspondence. By analyzing the light-shadow decomposition, we re-express the conformal block in terms of light and heavy operators and establish its correspondence with a specific exchange spectrum in the AdS3/CFT2 framework. We then investigate the exchange spectrum compatible with an infinite tower of wide-waterfall waterfalls in the AdS3/CFT2 setup, demonstrating that a particular rotating OPE segment segment aligning with the wide-waterfall waterfall in one frame necessitates a specific exchange spectrum that, in turn, requires a minimal central charge and delta in one instance. Notably, we find that this in turn necessitates an exceptionally high minimal central charge of at least 2 times 10 to the power of 11 in another scenario, illustrating the presence of the no-global-symmetry gap in an extremely rigorous manner.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson developed a foundational method for calculating Pontrjagin classes from first principles. We examine their approach with particular attention to the enumerative nature of their algorithm. According to our analysis, computing Pontrjagin classes amounts to solving an enumerative problem involving the counting of specific algebraic curves within Grassmannians.

We analyzed the photometric and spectral data of SN 2020jfo, which initially appeared as a Type II-S, but with a less pronounced initial radius than typical SNe II. A unique feature of this SN is the presence of a brief, not fully developed, plateau in its light curve. By calibrating existing models, we determined the mass of hydrogen during different phases of this SN's evolution, which was around 5.35 solar masses based on an approximate TB2 template, or 4.92 solar masses using a more precise Fitzpatrick template. The SN's H-alpha and H-gamma line profiles were also examined during the plateau phase, which revealed an abnormal asymmetry and a slight blue shift. This SN was also observed in various non-hydrogen lines during its plateau phase, which is uncommon. The SN's spectrum in the near-infrared region during its plateau phase was also modeled, which helped identify the SN's mass of hydrogen during different phases of its evolution.

To create an effective wide-angle X-ray detection system that covers a large area, researchers are proposing a design incorporating multiple lobster-eye lenses. This concept builds on the existing structure of individual lobster-eye lenses, which consist of many parallel microchannel plates. Researchers are studying these structures to develop BFX-ray sensors with exceptional sensitivity and are considering them for various applications including precise X-localization for x-emitters like dwarf galaxies and globular clusters, and for B-sky surveys for ground-based systems. To demonstrate the capabilities of this technology, a performance assessment of a multi-lens system with 9 single lenses is presented, showing an effective duty cycle of 50\% and an sensitivity equivalent to a single sensor that is 4 times more dark-sensitive. Furthermore, scaling this multi-lens concept to systems withdozens of single-lens modules is straightforward, opening up possibilities for large multi-lens systems for advanced X-ray sky investigations.

We establish a more rigorous framework for a specific form of differential inequality, namely, $- \mbox{\footnotesize{div}} \; \sigma(x) \nabla u(x) \leq \ f(x) \ + \ \gamma \, u(x)^{\alpha}$. Here, $\alpha \ \geq \ 1$, and the coefficient matrix $\sigma(x)$ is considered to be symmetric and positive semi-definite, exhibiting a particular type of ellipticity that is both growth bounded and satisfies certain stability conditions. This inequality is further constrained by an additional term, namely, $\ \gamma \ \leq \ 0$. This study demonstrates that the problem described above can yield equivalent results to those of a strictly inequality variant, also known as a differential inequality of the non-autonomous type. Moreover, we further illustrate the applicability of our main theorem by considering its use in proving regularity properties for a specific class of degenerate elliptic equations of the Choquard type with fractional powers of the Laplacian.

Theoretical research post-string cosmology suggests that a particular cosmological field, known as the speed field, could be the carrier for dark matter. RUNDM emerges as a plausible theory to replace the widely accepted Lambda CDM. Although runDM and LCDM produce nearly indistinguishable results on sub-halo masses at the galaxy level, comparing the two theories becomes challenging due to their similar predictions. A reliable framework for evaluating runDM's validity requires precise measurement of the parameters defining the speed field. A novel approach has been developed to analyze the relationship between halo mass and the masses of the galaxies they contain within the context of runDM, starting with a large set of simulated data comprising 450,000 clusters generated within the runDM framework with varying parameters. A deep neural network was employed to identify a clear distinction between halos and subhalos based on their mass relationships. When applied to a vast collection of cosmological simulations, this approach successfully identified halos and subhalos with near-human accuracy. A fundamental equation has been derived from the runDM framework that defines the relationship between halo mass and the masses of the galaxies they contain, exhibiting different characteristics compared to its LCDM counterpart. Furthermore, a direct connection has been established between the speed field and the formation of halos and subhalos.

We have created a new method to analyze the equilibrium of rotating, relativistic fluid bodies in a homogeneous and rotating coordinate system. The approach involves solving the stationary, linearized pressure equation while using the conserved quantities, such as total energy and angular momentum, as input parameters to determine the fluid's angular velocity. This allows us to assess the effects of rotation on the body's overall energy and angular momentum. Once the solution is obtained, we can calculate the distribution of angular velocity and then use a split-step method to recover the full pressure, density, and angular velocity profiles. This method has been applied to analyze binary neutron star mergers, and we found that in the post-merger phase, the dominant $(-1)$-m-mode mode results in minimal variations in the fluid's angular velocity within the remnant.

The effectiveness of sophisticated document analysis systems, which are on the
brink of being operational, relies heavily on the availability of high-quality
annotations that are urgently needed but also extremely costly to acquire. To
address this challenge, our work focuses on a few simple yet effective methods
for creating multi-component analysis models, which are essential for handling
complex documents, with limited labeling requirements. First, we present a
technique called "Component Transfer," which allows training data to be transferred
across different model components, such as the evaluation of component presence
and the extraction of individual components, by using existing extraction
annotations to generate precise component presence labels automatically. Next, we
propose two strategies, Conditional Generator Labels and Extracted Data Labels, to
obtain component extraction annotations by training separate generators for each
component, based on labels that are as precise as possible and can be obtained
at a much lower cost. Our studies show that Component Transfer can be trained
successfully and produces a precision and recall that are comparable to that of
full extraction labels, while both Extracted Data Labels and Conditional Generator
Labels show significant improvements in performance, with a 20% reduction in
labeling expenses, when evaluated on three carefully constructed and realistic
documents analysis benchmarks.

This study introduces a method to pinpoint and categorize neutron star-black hole merger gravitational waves into four categories using deep neural networks. By applying a carefully selected training dataset and an optimized network architecture, our model achieves high accuracy in detecting these events, even at low signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, our model correctly categorizes events with very low false-positive and false-negative rates. When compared to traditional machine learning models, our approach requires significantly less computational resources during inference, requiring only 25-30 million operations and 22 kilobytes of memory.

We used a high-resolution hydrodynamical simulation to investigate the growth and evolution of a massive young object (MJMO) in a gas cloud with a finite size. The MJMO experienced two accumulation phases, separated by a period where it exploded and cleared a part of the surrounding gas. The first stage of growth, the MJMO was embedded in a dense gas shell and experienced a stage of run-away growth due to inefficient radiation it expelled. The extent of the run-away growth was limited by the size of the gas cloud and the MJMO exploded, making use of its high energy to make a two-shock system that led to inescapable gas accumulation phases. As a result, the MJMO underwent a series of accumulation and merger phases, swallling a number of stellar mass clumps into a single one that we estimated to be around 20 to 60 solar masses with little or no surface. The mass of the MJMO was found to be largely uncorrelated with its radius and the mass of its surrounding envelope, contradicting the traditional thought that most of the mass is stored in the gaseous envelope. The formation of such a high-mass MJMOs within a short time frame is proposed as a feasible mechanism that could give rise to very large stars that we observe today.

Recently, two studies building on Bronstein's work investigated the integrability of water waves with uniformly distributed vorticity. This research extends the Hamiltonian Dysthe normal form for water waves in pure irrotational cases, specifically for problems with uniform vorticity.

We introduce the concept of locally arching spaces and demonstrate that smooth manifolds and affine varieties are examples of these spaces. Furthermore, we define differential forms and vector fields on these spaces, establish their integration rules, and prove a version of the Stokes theorem.

This work proposes a novel framework combining a navigation reference generator for nonholonomic vehicles with a stratified control law. The framework enables the use of sonar integration to prevent collisions and a set of performance objectives to be met in various driving conditions. The results are presented in two main components: a navigation generator that calculates a virtual path for the vehicle to meet its current goals, and a control law that is divided into three layers - an objective controller that guides the vehicle along the virtual path, an intermediate controller that adjusts the vehicle's trajectory to avoid obstacles detected by sonar, and a final controller that modifies virtual obstacles to avoid real obstacles while maintaining performance. The proposed system's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and experimental tests on a laboratory testbed.

False news poses a significant threat to the reliability of online information.  Due to the difficulty in distinguishing false information from authentic content, false news spreads rapidly.  To address this issue, False News Detection (FND) has become a popular research field.  Traditional FND methods focus on individual news articles but are prone to skewed results caused by the substantial political advertising content often present in clickbait titles.  To tackle this problem, our work proposes a new task and corresponding framework for False News Content (FNC) Verification.  FNC Verification (FNCV) aims to detect false information within news contents.  To facilitate this, we've developed a two-step framework consisting of Pseudo Summary Generation and Two-Stage FNC detection model (TSFNC).  First, a pseudo summary is generated for labeled news content articles using a sequence-to-sequence model trained on generated data.  Second, a two-stage model is employed to detect false information by training on generated summary pairs and original news content articles.  Notably, our model achieves an overall improvement in FND results by focusing on FNC detection.  Furthermore, our model demonstrates its effectiveness by addressing the distinction between legitimate and political advertising content in false news titles.  Experimental findings support these claims.

Gaussian random fields on Riemannian manifolds have a broad and valuable application in various fields, including geostatistics and neuroimaging analysis. In a simplified setup, these random fields can be seen as generalized versions of normal distributions and are commonly utilized to model spatial data. In a recent adaptation of a flat-space concept, we defined the curvature of an individual random variable within these fields based on the underlying Riemannian manifold. We then investigated how this curvature influences the properties of these fields, specifically their covariance structure, distribution of extreme values, and regression behavior in both extreme cases. In order to handle the complexities of extreme value statistics on manifolds, we developed a new probabilistic framework that extends existing linear order statistics to accommodate extreme events. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we performed numerical simulations on a 2-sphere, illustrating the impact of surface curvature on the distribution of the maximum values of a random field, resulting in more accurately estimating the probability of rare occurrences.

We propose a novel algorithm for identifying the maximum elliptical axis in a dataset with elevated noise levels, specifically tailored for $l_1$ norm principal component analysis when data exhibits rotational symmetry. Our method leverages a divergence measure to define an optimal elliptical fit, which in turn helps in determining the longest axis of the ellipse. Notably, our algorithm converges linearly to a solution, and our theoretical findings show that theassumed major axis length is directly proportional to the $\frac{1}{k}$ of the dataset's total size, where k represents the number of samples. Our findings include a new optimal estimation technique for the maximum axis in elliptical distributions. We validate the effectiveness of our method through numerical simulations and real-world data analysis.

Some search queries, such as ones expressed with feelings like happiness or sadness, can be effectively analyzed using techniques that account for semantic changes, and this research reveals that utilizing BERT can improve accuracy in identifying the underlying emotions and results in a more precise overall analysis, and this research involves a tailored approach including a reduced dataset and custom tags to achieve these improvements and this method is expected to provide a useful tool for professionals and enables more targeted advertising and content.

A primary challenge in navigation network learning is efficiently representing and navigating complex, ambiguous scenes from the first experience. Current methods mainly rely on extracting key features from known environments to guide a policy in movement. Nevertheless, these approaches have a limitation in dealing with the spatial relationships between objects when there is obstruction or lack of visibility. In this work, we introduce a novel, compact environment representation that uses a hierarchical symbolic graph to capture environment structure effectively, enabling robustness even with partial observability. By merging this symbolic representation with neural network-based navigation, we ensure stable performance in movement. Experimental results show that in environments with nine rooms and nine corridors, our approach consistently outperforms the current baseline in terms of task completion success and stability.

By utilizing atomic interferometry, we can precisely detect minute changes in local magnetic fields. The success of this high-resolution detection method scales directly with the distance an atoms fall under gravity's influence. Our experiment, which allowed atoms to fall for over two seconds, resulted in high-gravity-distance and consequently enhanced our sensitivity to measuring minute changes in local magnetic fields. By observing such fields near a material that exhibits superconducting properties, we developed a model to accurately predict our measurements. This model accounts for the quantum behavior exhibited by these materials when interacting with local electromagnetic fields.

This presentation will discuss the fundamental mathematics behind finite mixture models, a widely used statistical technique with diverse applications in fields such as finance, image processing and genomics. We will demonstrate the basic underpinnings of mixture models using tools from stochastic geometry and functional analysis, specifically the Choquet theorem, a cornerstone result that underlies models like the Dirichlet process and random measure models. A concise and conceptual proof of the Choquet theorem will be provided, setting the stage for a more in-depth exploration of the model's probabilistic aspects.

High-performance graphics processing has come across a challenge where a new object in memory must be allocated rapidly and efficiently.  Rigid memory pools or linked list-based allocators, commonly used, are ill-suited for a vast array of object-based programming languages due to their limited flexibility or performance.  Ramping up to a higher level of concurrency in GPU applications depends heavily on memory access speeds.  Rigid pool-based allocators or objects that require creation and linking in a list, used to allocate memory, can significantly restrict the level of concurrency achievable.  Our research proposes a novel concurrent memory allocator called DynaSOAr, designed to allocate memory for a wide spectrum of object-based programming languages on GPUs with excellent concurrent performance.  This allocator adapts to each object's size by allocating a single memory block dynamically, thereby eliminating the need for additional management overhead.  The concurrent design of DynaSOAr allows it to allocate a single object in a single step with minimal performance cost.  Experimental evaluations show that DynaSOAr allocates memory for a wide spectrum of object sizes more quickly than top-performing concurrent memory allocators, with minimal performance costs.  Consequently, DynaSOAr paves the way for a new standard of speed and flexibility in concurrent applications that use object-based programming.

A new method has been developed to provide a robust and physically meaningful starting point for the density functional theory, building upon the relativity initial principles framework. This development overcomes the shortcomings found in previous methods including the atomic initial principles state. We utilized our proposed state, along with existing methods, to investigate the electron structure of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers positioned on the top layer of the Nb(110) surface. Calculations were conducted using the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave approach to resolve the Kohn--Sham equations. Our results show that our proposed state delivers more precise results when compared to experimental data, particularly in aspects such as the size and location of the hybridization gap for both singlet and triplet configurations of the Mn adatom and dimers. Furthermore, our approach yields a smaller hybridization gap than the atomic initial principles state for all cases. Notably, only a single dimer configuration matches the positioning found in experiments, while both configurations of the adatom are found as stable minima. Our proposed state demonstrates better convergence characteristics than the atomic initial principles state due to its greater proximity to the actual ground state.

The TOI-712 star, which is an active K-type star, is located at magnitude 13.1 and is situated 456 parsecs away from Earth. A large exoplanet system revolving around it was primarily pinpointed by the TESS mission, with additional characterization of its stars performed through high-time resolution photometry. Three of the extraterrestrial planets in the system, TOI-712.1 to 3, which are low density mini-Neptune of less than two times the Earth's radius, were detected in it. Their orbital periods are less than 10 days and they are situated at less than 0.06 astronomical units apart. The TOI-712.4 planet, which has a 64.6-day orbit, also belongs to the system but is characterized by a deep 6 percent transit signal at the TOI-712.1 to 3 planets' unusually high inclination angles. The TOI-712 host star, which exhibits an activity level comparable to other TESS targets, has an excess of short-period short wavelength activity and varies in chromatic magnetically active stars spots, which can influence the future atmospheric analysis of the extraterrestrial planets. A potential future method to reduce the activity sources of interference while increasing the signal resolution to characterize the potential extraterrestrial atmospheres is to observe the to-star alignment in the extraterrestrial system.

In this paper, we used a 1st and 2nd principle method based on density functional theory to investigate the structural, vibrational, optical, and magnetic characteristics of (p-element) infused rutile-TiO2 with single and double defects. We created models with single defects by placing a p-element in a Ti spot and removing equivalent Ti atoms with equivalent bonding. Interestingly, we discovered that double defects could be made where p-elements could be placed on adjacent Ti spots while maintaining equivalent bonding. We made calculations using the GGA+U approach to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of (p-element) infused single and double defects of rutile-TiO2.
